Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and alert you when hypertension may be present, but they don't give you actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices can do this, but they need to be calibrated regularly with a traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to offer full blood pressure measurement without any calibration, citing clinical trial results involving thousands of participants…

The silent killer

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) both pose serious health risks.

Of the two, hypertension is more dangerous and is even called "the silent killer"—it can cause serious and irreversible damage to your arteries, heart and brain, yet has no obvious symptoms. Many people only discover they have the condition after a heart attack or stroke.

For elderly people, measuring blood pressure regularly is ideal. Although there are many easy-to-use home upper-arm blood pressure monitors on the market, it would be even better to have a fitness device that can be worn all day and monitor automatically.

Apple Watch blood pressure feature

With the launch of watchOS 26, five Apple Watch models can now measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these models won't provide any readings—they only issue alerts when signs of possible hypertension are detected. Other devices like the Oura Ring work in a similar way.

Some fitness devices on the market can provide actual blood pressure readings, but they need to be calibrated regularly with readings from an upper-arm blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup Vital Signals says its Signal Ring smart ring requires no calibration, yet can measure with accuracy comparable to traditional upper-arm blood pressure monitors.

CEO Tom Moss told Bloomberg that he himself nearly died from undiagnosed hypertension—an experience that prompted him to found the company.

The Signal Ring will open for orders later today, ship in October, and is priced at US$399 with no subscription required. The companion smartphone app can display real-time blood pressure readings and long-term trends (as shown in the image above).

Worth noting is that the Oura Ring has not yet received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), although clinical trials show it can deliver accurate blood pressure readings for thousands of participants.

Interestingly, Moss himself isn't particularly keen on marketing the Signal Ring to all consumers. He says the feature is best suited for elderly people and those assessed by a doctor as being at risk of hypertension—comments that suggest the Signal Ring may not be particularly outstanding in other areas (such as sleep tracking).
